title: The Quiet Ten Minutes
passage:
Every afternoon, the student council office became noisy. Members arrived from different clubs, asked questions, searched for papers, and tried to finish several tasks at once. Meetings often began late because nobody was sure what needed to be done first. Mei, the council secretary, suggested an experiment. For the first ten minutes after school, nobody would hold a meeting. Instead, each person would quietly check the task board, prepare necessary materials, and write one clear goal for the day. Some members thought the rule would waste valuable time. They wanted to start discussing problems immediately. Mei asked them to try it for one week before deciding. On the first day, the room felt strangely silent. One student found that a form he planned to discuss had already been answered by a teacher. Another noticed that two members were preparing the same poster. Because they checked the task board first, they divided the work before the meeting began. By the third day, meetings were starting earlier and ending sooner. The group also added a small section to the board called Waiting For. Tasks that could not continue until someone gave information were placed there. This stopped members from repeatedly asking about work that was temporarily blocked. At the end of the week, the council compared the number of unfinished tasks with the previous week. The difference was not huge, but members reported feeling less rushed. More importantly, they could explain what they had accomplished each day. Mei pointed out that the ten quiet minutes did not reduce work time; they prevented some work from being repeated or started without the right information. The council kept the practice but made it flexible. Before special events, when urgent decisions were necessary, they shortened the quiet period. This taught Mei another lesson: a useful routine should support a goal, not become a rule that people follow without thinking. The success of the experiment came from creating a short pause between arriving and acting. That pause gave everyone time to see the whole situation before choosing the next step. Mei later used the same habit while studying. Before opening a textbook, she spent a few minutes deciding exactly what she wanted to finish. She found that a small amount of planning often saved more time than it cost.

The council also tested what happened when the quiet period was skipped for three days during a busy week. At first, members felt they were saving time, but duplicate questions and missing materials increased again. The comparison helped them understand that the routine was useful because it reduced switching between tasks. Still, Mei warned against turning the ten minutes into another complicated meeting. The preparation period worked only when it remained simple: check the board, gather what was needed, and choose one priority. By keeping the purpose clear, the council avoided adding extra forms or rules. Mei learned that an effective routine often succeeds not because it contains many steps, but because it protects a small amount of attention before work becomes busy.
translation:
毎日の放課後、生徒会室は騒がしくなっていました。さまざまな部活から来たメンバーが質問し、書類を探し、複数の作業を同時に始めるため、会議も遅れがちでした。書記の芽衣は、最初の十分間は会議をせず、各自が静かに作業表を確認し、必要な資料を準備し、その日の目標を一つ書く方法を提案しました。時間の無駄だという意見もありましたが、一週間だけ試すことにしました。初日、一人は話し合う予定だった書類にすでに先生の回答があることに気づき、別の二人は同じポスターを重複して作ろうとしていることに気づきました。三日目には会議の開始が早まり、終了も早くなりました。さらに『返答待ち』という欄を作り、誰かの情報が来るまで進められない仕事を分けたことで、止まっている仕事について何度も確認する無駄も減りました。一週間後、未完了の仕事数が劇的に減ったわけではありませんが、メンバーは以前ほど急かされる感覚がなく、その日に何を終えたか説明しやすくなりました。静かな十分間は作業時間を奪うのではなく、重複や情報不足のまま始める作業を防いでいたのです。ただし特別行事前など緊急時には短縮することにしました。芽衣は、習慣は目的を助けるために使うもので、考えず守る規則にしてはいけないとも学びました。到着してすぐ動く前に短い間を置くことで、全体を見て次の行動を選べます。芽衣は勉強でも同じ方法を使い、教科書を開く前に数分だけ『何を終えるか』を決めるようになりました。少しの計画が、それ以上の時間を節約することがあると分かったのです。

忙しい週に三日間だけ静かな十分間を省く実験もしました。時間を節約できるように見えましたが、重複した質問や資料不足が再び増えました。一方で、準備時間を複雑な会議にしてはいけないとも分かりました。作業表を見る、必要な物をそろえる、優先事項を一つ決めるという単純さが、忙しくなる前の注意を守る働きをしていたのです。
